GPU speed up for pcg() is disappointing - MATLAB Answers - MATLAB Central. x = pcg(A, b, tol, 5000, A);. To me, this looks like pcg() is actually choosing to do x=A\b (it itakes exactly the same amount of time as A\b). If pcg() also tries to do A\b directly on the GPU then this would explain the stall given that backslash does not parralise well. "To me, this looks like pcg() is actually choosing to do x=A\b (it itakes exactly the same amount of time as A\b). If M is A, the A\*inv(M) is identity matrix (cond=1), the pcg converges in one iteration but it shift the calculation to (M \ pk) which is (A \ pk), and pk is b! If you pass a preconditioner to GPU PCG then it is decomposed using ILU and the triangular factors used to perform the preconditioning. x = pcg(gpuArray(A), b, tol, 5000, L, L');. Unfortunately base MATLAB does not support single precision sparse and therefore neither does the GPU. >> tic; pcg(gpuArray(A),b,tol,5000,L\*L'); toc. In R2024b, coming out in a few weeks, we have added support for two triangular preconditioners to the GPU sparse solvers. >> tic; pcg(gpuArray(A),b,tol,50000,L,L'); toc. Preconditioner input for sparse input is only supported for a single preconditioner matrix, not two as in the CPU case. Perhaps you could try to use the GPU version with a dense (non-sparse) input - it's wasteful in memory but perhaps possibly faster than the sparse-CPU version:. x = pcg(gpuArray(double(A)), b, tol, 5000, L, L');. \* Only one sparse matrix preconditioner M1 is supported. pcg(gpuArray(A),b,[],[],@(x)L\x,@(x)L'\x). pcg(gpuArray(A),b,[],[],@(x)L\x,@(x)L'\x). pcg(gpuArray(A),b,[],[],@(x)L\double(x),@(x)L'\double(x)). pcg(gpuArray(A),b,[],[],@(x)gather(L)\double(x),@(x)gather(L')\double(x)). pcg(gpuArray(A),b,[],[],@(x)L\full(x),@(x)L'\full(x)). I agree, I think pcg() for sparse inputs on the GPU needs an update to match the good performance of the CPU version. tic; x = pcg(A, b, tol, 5000, L, L'); toc; %this runs on the CPU and takes ~16s. 1. CPU version of pcg() with L: 347 iterations, 16 sec. 2. CPU version of pcg() without L: 7285 iterations, 106 sec. 3. GPU version of pcg() with L: does not work. 4. GPU version of pcg() without L: 7281 iterations, 14 sec. x = pcg(A, b, tol, 5000, @(y) L\y, @(y)L'\y);.

### your communities. ### more stack exchange communities. ##### Collectives™ on Stack Overflow. # [Sparse Cholesky factorization algorithm for GPU [closed]](/questions/7123101/sparse-cholesky-factorization-algorithm-for-gpu). Can anyone provide me with a parallel algorithm for calculating the sparse Cholesky factorization? It must be suitable for execution on a GPU. Jonathan DeCarlo's user avatar. Generally speaking, direct sparse methods are not a great fit for the GPU. While the best direct solvers (thinking about packages like CHOLMOD, SuperLU, MUMPS here) use strategies to generate dense sub blocks which can be processed using L3 BLAS, the size and shape of the blocks don't tend to profit from using a GPU BLAS for acceleration. Seeing as you are asking about a sparse Cholesky factorization, I assumed the matrix is symmetric positive definite. In that case you might consider using an iterative solver -- there are a number of good implementations of Conjugate Gradient and other Krylov subspace methods with simple preconditioners which might be of some use. The multi-frontal algorithm seems to be a popular choice for parallel sparse factorisation. I would investigate whether it's possible to link to a `GPU` based `BLAS` implementation, such as `CUDA BLAS` or the like if you're keen to use your `GPU` rather than `FPU`. Contrary to dense factorisation, sparse methods always include a non-negligible amount of integer work in addition to the floating-point work done (though the floating-point is still dominant). I'm no expert on `GPU's`, but would the `CPU` be better suited for integer work than the `GPU`?? This might be an argument against implementing the whole algorithm for the `GPU`... Darren Engwirda's user avatar. Linear Programming on a GPU. this might not be a computation where you see a lot of benefit from using the GPU. Sparse Cholesky factorizations on a GPU is an open problem. Even the Linear Programming paper mentioned previously uses a dense algorithm while most problems are sparse. The commercial LP solver market is very competitive, but nobody has a product that makes much use of the GPU yet. David Nehme's user avatar. Title: Computation and memory issues of cholesky and cholesky_inverse - PyTorch Forums
# Computation and memory issues of cholesky and cholesky\_inverse. Hi, I’ve been looking into `torch.cholesky` and `torch.cholesky_inverse` for large matrices and have experienced some problems with them. When I run the following script:. A = torch.randn(30000, 40000, device='cuda'). %time L = torch.cholesky(A). %time A_inv = torch.cholesky_inverse(L)`. `CPU times: user 24.5 s, sys: 352 ms, total: 24.9 s. CPU times: user 3min 36s, sys: 969 ms, total: 3min 37s. Wall time: 42.7 s`. I’m really confused about the long run time of `cholesky_inverse`. As I understand it computes `L_inv.t() @ L_inv` and `L_inv` should be computed in O(n^2) time as `L` is a lower triangular matrix. However, it’s running much longer than the cholesky factorization which needs O(n^3) time. With these sizes, I would expect `cholesky_inverse` to take an instant. My another doubt is about the memory consumption of `cholesky`. I thought that if I do `torch.cholesky(A, out=A)` on a 50000 x 50000 float matrix `A` (9.31GB) then I should not run out of memory on a 12GB GPU. However, I can see that pytorch tries to allocate another 9.31GB which throws an OOM error. My guess is that even though Cholesky decomposition can be calculated in-place, the corresponding MAGMA routine doesn’t do exactly that and allocates another 9.31 GB of memory for performance reasons? `torch.cholesky(A, out=A)`. I realized that the very slow run times were due to another user occupying the GPU node and using up all the CPU resources. Now for the same setup cholesky takes ~2.5s and the cholesky\_inverse takes ~0.6s (still I would expect it would be faster, but it’s not a problem now). I’m still however wondering if it’s possible to perform Cholesky inplace without allocating extra memory? I forgot about CUDA asynchronous calls and thus the timings were wrongs. I added cuda.synchronize and ran the following code:. A = torch.randn(30000, 35000, device='cuda'). print('torch.inverse', time() - t). torch.cholesky(A, out=A). print('torch.cholesky', time() - t). torch.cholesky_inverse(A, out=A). print('torch.cholesky_inverse', time() - t)`. So again, `cholesky_inverse` takes extremely long. I would expect it to be many times faster than `cholesky` but it doesn’t seem to be the case. I am not sure how to explain this though :confused:.

results.content: # Solving sparse matrix on GPU and memory problems (even with free memory available). I am running a backslash computation A\b where A is an array of type sparse and b is a vector, both stored as gpuArrays. In fact, the size of A is only 50Mb and the GPU is a Nvidia GTX 1050, 4Gb. Following is the result of a gpuDevice call after this error:. It seems that this is an issue with the backslash operator since both A and b can be stored on the GPU without problems. Any thoughts on how to solve large sparse systems on the GPU? So it's a sparse array A and a vector b, both stored in the GPU. Perhaps this specific GPU is not able to perform these operations using double arrays? I must admit, I'm not extremely familiar with the behaviour of the matrix factorization we use to implement the sparse direct solve; however it wouldn't surprise me if the result is quite dense. sol= pcg(KGR\_gpu,FR\_gpu,1e-1,1e6,L,L');. For the time being this same code runs whenever matrix KGR and vector FR are not stored at the GPU. Error using gpuArray/pcg (line 58) When the first input argument is a sparse matrix, the second preconditioner cannot be a matrix. The problem is solved (not yet - please check Joss comments) with preallocation on the GPU:. KGR\_gpu=gpuArray(sparse(n,n)) % where n is the order of KGR\_gpu. Since I am using a Nvidia GTX 1050 (not suitable for double precision) the backslash with KGR\_gpu and KGR are almost equivalent in time:. KGR\_gpu=gpuArray(sparse(n,n)) % where n is the order of KGR\_gpu. After this code, KGR\_gpu and KGR are the same CPU array and the computation will happen on the CPU in both cases. KGR\_gpu=gpuArray(sparse(length(KGR),length(KGR)));. This is still very strange since KGR has only 0.20Gb and the GPU is a GTX 1050 with 4Gb. I will post updates of this same computation with an iterative solver. sol=pcg(KGR\_gpu,FR,1e-5,1e5);. pcg(KGR\_gpu, FR, 1e-5, 1e5, KGR\_gpu);. The GPU solvers (currently) use ILU to factorize the matrix and attempt to precondition the system. What still amazes me is the fact that a 0.20Gb matrix can't be solved using the backslash operator in a nominal 4Gb GPU.
